purpose: Nafcillin is an antibiotic used to treat serious bacterial infections, especially those caused by a germ called Staphylococcus aureus (staph). It is commonly used for skin infections, bone infections, heart valve infections, and bloodstream infections. It works specifically against staph bacteria that are resistant to regular penicillin.
how_it_works: Nafcillin works by attacking the outer wall of bacteria, which they need to survive. It blocks the bacteria from building and repairing that wall, causing the bacteria to fall apart and die. Think of it like removing the bricks from a building so it eventually collapses — the antibiotic does that to the bacteria.
common_side_effects: Pain, redness, or irritation at the injection site are very common since this medicine is usually given through an IV. You may also experience nausea, diarrhea, or an upset stomach. Some people develop a skin rash. It can also cause low potassium levels in your blood, which your doctor will watch for.
warnings: Tell your doctor right away if you have ever had an allergic reaction to penicillin or similar antibiotics like amoxicillin, as nafcillin can cause a serious allergic reaction. Watch for signs of allergy such as hives, swelling, or difficulty breathing. This medication can affect your liver, so let your doctor know if you have liver problems. It can also cause a serious colon infection called C. diff — contact your doctor if you develop severe or bloody diarrhea.
typical_dosing: Nafcillin is almost always given as an IV (intravenous) injection in a hospital or clinic setting — it is not taken by mouth. The typical adult dose is 1 to 2 grams given every 4 to 6 hours, depending on how serious the infection is. Your doctor will decide the right dose and how long you need to take it based on your specific infection.
